name: BPRC
description: The Biomedical Primate Research Centre (BPRC) in Rijswijk, the Netherlands, is a not-for-profit research institute that works with non-human primate models. Its tuberculosis research uses macaques to test new tuberculosis vaccines and treatments against the current BCG vaccine, measuring safety, immune responses and protection. Its macaque tuberculosis work is related to the IMPAcTb program.
research_focus: Non-human primate models of tuberculosis; testing of BCG and new tuberculosis vaccine and therapy candidates in macaques
tags: BPRC, Biomedical Primate Research Centre, Rijswijk, macaque, rhesus macaque, non-human primate, NHP, tuberculosis, TB, BCG, vaccine

name: Break Through Cancer
description: Break Through Cancer's glioblastoma TeamLab, 'Accelerating GBM Therapies Through Serial Biopsies', is a foundation-funded collaboration of Dana-Farber, Brigham and Women's, Johns Hopkins, Memorial Sloan Kettering, MD Anderson and MIT's Koch Institute. The team takes repeated (serial) biopsies from the same glioblastoma patients to learn whether a therapy reaches the tumor and has its intended effect, and tests whether cerebrospinal fluid and blood can serve as surrogate markers. Tumor samples are profiled with sequencing, proteomics, imaging and spatial methods. It is separate from CSBC, the NCI-funded glioblastoma center at MIT and Dana-Farber.
research_focus: Recurrent glioblastoma; serial brain biopsies to test whether a therapy reaches the tumor and acts on target; single-cell, proteomic, immunopeptidomic and spatial profiling; cerebrospinal fluid and blood as surrogate markers of drug activity
key_data_types: Short- and long-read DNA sequencing with copy number analysis
Mass spectrometry proteomics, phosphoproteomics and immunopeptidomics
Clinical oncopanel and proximity extension assays
tags: Break Through Cancer, BTC, GBM, glioblastoma, recurrent glioblastoma, serial biopsy, TeamLab, Dana-Farber, DFCI, Koch Institute, CAN-3110, oncolytic virus, spatial transcriptomics

name: CSBC
alternative_names: Center for Systems Biology of Glioblastoma
pi: White, Forest M. (MIT, contact PI); Michor, Franziska (Dana-Farber, co-PI)
description: The MIT/Dana-Farber Center for Systems Biology of Glioblastoma is an NCI U54 center in the Cancer Systems Biology Consortium, led by Forest White (MIT) and Franziska Michor (Dana-Farber). It studies how neurons, immune cells and tumor cells interact in glioblastoma, and why the tumor microenvironment suppresses immune responses. The team combines patient tumor samples, mouse and patient-derived xenograft models and mass spectrometry proteomics with computational and multi-scale models to find therapeutic targets. It is separate from the Break Through Cancer glioblastoma TeamLab.
research_focus: Quantitative systems biology of glioblastoma; tumor-neural-immune interactions in the GBM microenvironment; integrated computational and multi-scale modeling to identify therapeutic strategies
key_data_types: Tissue sections with cyclic immunofluorescence (CyCIF) imaging

name: Griffith
pi: Griffith, Linda G. (MIT, PI; Scientific Director, Center for Gynepathology Research); Goods, Brittany A. (University of Melbourne, partner lab)
description: Endometriosis and uterine biology research from Linda Griffith's lab at MIT, working with Brittany Goods' lab, and from the multi-lab Center for Gynepathology Research that Griffith directs. The work grows patient-derived endometrial organoids and stromal co-cultures in synthetic hydrogels to model the endometrium across the menstrual cycle, and profiles patient tissue with single-cell RNA sequencing and proteomics to find the molecular features of endometriosis and adenomyosis. It is funded by NIH (NICHD, and earlier NIBIB).
research_focus: Endometriosis and adenomyosis; the human endometrium across the menstrual cycle; patient-derived endometrial organoid and stromal co-cultures in synthetic hydrogels; single-cell RNA-seq and proteomic profiles of endometriosis

name: Impact
pi: Fortune, Sarah M. (Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, contact PI); Flynn, JoAnne L. (U Pittsburgh, co-lead); Boom, W. Henry (Case Western Reserve, co-lead); Bryson, Bryan (MIT, member lab); Lauffenburger, Douglas A. (MIT, member lab); Shalek, Alex K. (MIT, member lab)
description: Hi-IMPAcTB is a multi-center tuberculosis consortium funded by NIAID as one of its Immune Mechanisms of Protection Against Mycobacterium tuberculosis (IMPAc-TB) centers, led by Sarah Fortune (Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health) with co-leads JoAnne Flynn (University of Pittsburgh) and W. Henry Boom (Case Western Reserve). It studies which immune responses to Mycobacterium tuberculosis protect against infection and disease, to guide vaccine and diagnostic design. The consortium collects multi-modal data from lungs and blood in mice, non-human primates and humans, including flow and mass cytometry, single-cell sequencing, systems serology, PET/CT imaging and barcoded Mtb strains.
research_focus: Host-pathogen interactions in tuberculosis; characterizing protective vs. non-protective immunological responses to Mycobacterium tuberculosis to inform vaccine design
key_data_types: Systems serology (antibody titers, Fc receptor binding, antibody-dependent functional assays, Luminex)
NHP, mouse and human tissue and granuloma samples
Bacterial samples and digitally barcoded Mtb

name: MetNet
pi: Kamm, Roger D. (MIT, contact PI); Shenoy, Vivek B. (UPenn, co-PI)
description: The MIT MetNet Center is an NCI U54 center in the Metastasis Research Network, led by Roger Kamm (MIT) and Vivek Shenoy (University of Pennsylvania). It studies how mechanical and molecular stresses drive metastatic colonization, dormancy and outgrowth in different organs, including how circulating tumor cells adapt as they leave the blood vessels. The team combines engineered microvascular and organ-on-chip models, in vivo models and computational modeling to identify anti-metastatic therapeutic strategies.
research_focus: Mechanical determinants of metastatic cancer colonization, dormancy, and outgrowth; mechano-adaptation of circulating tumor cells during extravasation and organ-selective colonization
key_data_types: Cell and device imaging with image analysis
Extravasation, migration, permeability and clot assays
RNA sequencing and chromatin sequencing analysis

It provides sequencing library preparation, high-throughput sequencing, single-cell and spatial genomics, bioinformatics analysis and data management to labs across MIT. name: NAMs
alternative_names: NAMs Technology Development Center for Women's Health
description: The MIT NAMs Technology Development Center for Women's Health, directed by Linda Griffith within the Center for Gynepathology Research, develops new approach methodologies (NAMs) to make drug development for gynecologic diseases easier. It builds human microphysiological systems of reproductive tissues and the liver, guided by computational systems biology and clinical data, and benchmarks them against patient data for endometriosis, adenomyosis, heavy menstrual bleeding and polycystic ovary syndrome. It is funded by NCATS through the NIH Common Fund's Complement-ARIE program and works with industry partners on preclinical use cases.
research_focus: New approach methodologies; microphysiological systems and organ-on-chip models of gynecologic disease (endometriosis, adenomyosis, heavy menstrual bleeding, PCOS); computational systems biology; drug metabolism and safety models

name: RMS-NGC
pi: Koehler, Angela N. (MIT Koch Institute and Broad Institute, contact PI); Burgin, Alex B.; Gould, Alexandra E.; Linardic, Corinne M.; Nomura, Daniel (multi-PIs)
description: An NCI Next Generation Chemistry Center at MIT, led by Angela Koehler with Alex Burgin, Alexandra Gould, Corinne Linardic and Daniel Nomura, that looks for drugs against fusion-positive alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma, a childhood cancer driven by the PAX3-FOXO1 fusion protein. Its projects look for small molecules that bind PAX3-FOXO1, degraders that remove it, and ways to target the transcriptional complex it works with, using medicinal chemistry, chemical biology and chemoproteomics. It is part of NCI's Targeting Fusion Oncoproteins in Childhood Cancers (TFCC) network.
research_focus: Fusion-positive alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma; PAX3-FOXO1 fusion oncoprotein; small-molecule discovery, targeted degraders (PROTACs, molecular glues) and chemoproteomics
tags: RMS-NGC, rhabdomyosarcoma, RMS, alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma, fusion-positive, PAX3-FOXO1, fusion oncoprotein, Next Generation Chemistry Center, NGC, TFCC, Koehler, Angela, Koch Institute, Broad Institute, Broad, small molecule, PROTAC, molecular glue, degrader, chemoproteomics, UM1CA294108

name: Shoulders
description: Research from Matthew Shoulders' lab in MIT Chemistry, which studies how cells fold proteins and how proteostasis networks, such as chaperones and endoplasmic reticulum quality control, shape protein function and evolution. A main direction is collagen proteostasis in health and disease: how procollagen is folded and checked, and how disease variants disrupt it, studied in human cartilage (chondronoids) grown from iPSCs and profiled by imaging, RNA sequencing and mass spectrometry proteomics. It is funded by NIAMS.
research_focus: Protein folding and proteostasis; collagen folding and ER quality control of procollagen; collagen disease variants (such as COL2A1 in osteoarthritis) in iPSC-derived cartilage models; chaperones and protein evolution
tags: Shoulders, Shoulders Lab, collagen, Collagen Study, COL2A1, procollagen, proteostasis, protein folding, ER quality control, osteoarthritis, cartilage, chondronoid, iPSC, R01AR082995

name: SRP
description: The MIT Superfund Research Program, an NIEHS-funded P42 center led by Bevin Engelward, studies the health risks of N-nitrosamines and other hazardous chemicals in drinking water, at the Olin Chemical Superfund Site in Wilmington, Massachusetts, and beyond. It combines engineering, biology and community engagement: sensors that detect contaminants, mouse and cell studies of DNA damage, mutation and cancer risk, and technologies that clean contaminated water. It works with affected communities, including Wilmington and the Passamaquoddy Tribe.
research_focus: Environmental health impacts of N-nitrosamines; hazardous chemical sensing, mutagenicity, cancer risk, and remediation of contaminated drinking water in affected communities (Wilmington, MA and Passamaquoddy Tribe)
key_data_types: Mouse nitrosamine exposure studies (tissues, histopathology, GPT assays)
DNA damage and mutation assays (CometChip, RaDR imaging, mutational spectra sequencing)
Chemical synthesis and characterization (NMR, spectroscopy, crystallography)
tags: SRP, MIT SRP, Superfund, Superfund Research Program, NIEHS, P42, P42ES027707, Engelward, N-nitrosamines, nitrosamine, drinking water, water quality, DNA damage, mutagenesis, CometChip
